newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU SAYS BEEF EXPORTS BROKE MAD COW BAN.
newsitem.headline: EU SAYS BEEF EXPORTS BROKE MAD COW BAN.

text.p: The European Commission said on Thursday that 1,600 tonnes of British beef had been exported illegally, with Belgian help, to the Netherlands, Russia and Egypt despite a ban imposed because of the mad cow crisis.

Following media reports and under mounting consumer pressure to come clean, the EU's executive disclosed that the quantity of British beef smuggled out of the country was more than double initial estimates.
"With the complicity of Belgian operators this beef was fraudulently declared to be of Belgian origin," Commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas told a news briefing.
Van der Pas later said that two Belgian companies, believed to be involved in the fraud, were searched on Thursday but he was unaware of any arrests.
Belgium is considered to be the hub of a European black market trade in hormone-treated meat. Two years ago a Belgian veterinary inspector was shot dead by members of the Flemish-based beef "mafia."

The EU Commission said the illegal exports of British beef only came to light following an EU veterinary inspectors' mission last week to Britain. Their report was distributed at a meeting of senior EU veterinary officials on Thursday.

But the German newspaper, Frankfurter Rundschau, said in a faxed copy of a story due to be published on Friday that in April Dutch customs officials confiscated 900 tonnes of British beef in the Dutch port of Vlissingen.
Van der Pas said that the Dutch had sounded the alarm several weeks ago and that the Commission's anti-fraud squad had been investigating.
Asked why the fraud had not been disclosed earlier, Van der Pas said: "We couldn't go public because we didn't have all the elements and the investigation would have been endangered."
At the midday news briefing, Van der Pas said 700 tonnes had been seized by Dutch authorities and the remaining 900 tonnes had probably been exported to Russia and Egypt.
"If this information is confirmed the illegally exported British beef has not been exported to the markets of EU member states," he said.

Van der Pas denied press reports that British beef had been fraudulently marketed in France and Spain and could not confirm reports of exports to other countries such as Bosnia. Although exporters of the beef to Russia and Egypt were believed to be French and Spanish, the meat could have been bought from Dutch stores for direct shipment to non-EU countries, he said.
It was perfectly possible they acted in good faith believing that the beef was Belgian, he added.

An Agriculture Ministry spokewoman in London said Britain was aware of allegations that hundreds of tonnes of its beef had been illegally exported and had been investigating them even before the European Commission revealed them.
"Action will be taken if the allegations are proved to be correct," the spokeswoman said.

The Commission said on Wednesday it was considering legal action against Britain over the exports. The ban was imposed in March 1996 to protect consumers after the British government said it was possible a human form of the fatal mad cow disease could be caught from eating infected beef.
But the Commission sparked outrage by refusing to say how much beef was involved and to which countries it had been exported, arguing that this would hinder legal inquiries.

In reponse to a question if legal action could extend beyond Britain, Van der Pas said that if the origin of British beef had been changed, then this was a crime which member states should crack down on. "It's up to the member states to act and if the Belgian side of things becomes clear, and we think it will become clear very quickly, it will be a matter for Belgian authorities," he said.
